title: Other religions (Nostra Aetate, 1965)
hook: the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions

segments.voice: Yesterday, ecumenism: the search for unity among Christians. Your line was that they may be one. Today, a wider circle.

Athens, the first century. Paul walks through the city and sees altars everywhere, one with an inscription: to the unknown god. Invited to speak on the Areopagus, a hill where the city's thinkers gathered, he doesn't mock their altars. He starts from one of them and reaches for words they already know. "For in him we live, and move, and are," he says, and adds that some of their poets had said we are God's offspring. Nineteen centuries later, the Catholic Church wrote a short document about people of other religions, and it sounds a lot like Paul on that hill.
screen: `ATHENS: TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.` → `PAUL STARTS FROM THEIR ALTAR.` → `NINETEEN CENTURIES LATER.`

segments.voice: In 1965 the Second Vatican Council issued a declaration named by its first Latin words: Nostra Aetate, in our age. Its central sentence: the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions. It speaks with sincere respect of their ways of living and acting and their teachings, which, it says, often reflect a ray of the truth that enlightens all people. It names Hindus and Buddhists and their searching, and speaks with esteem of Muslims, who worship the one God and honor Abraham, Jesus as a prophet, and Mary. The same document says the Church also keeps proclaiming Christ, and holds both together. A whole section is about the Jewish people. It speaks of the great spiritual heritage Christians share with them. It says that what happened in Christ's passion cannot be charged against all the Jews of that time, or against Jews today. And it deplores hatred and antisemitism at any time and from any source. After centuries of that charge, those sentences were written down at a council. In 1986, Pope John Paul II invited leaders of many religions to Assisi to pray for peace, each in their own way, side by side. The Church asks Catholics to meet their neighbors of other faiths with respect, to learn, and to work together for the good. Nothing true is rejected: not because every belief is the same, but because truth, wherever it's found, is taken seriously.
screen: `NOSTRA AETATE: IN OUR AGE.` · `NOTHING TRUE AND HOLY REJECTED.` · `NO COLLECTIVE BLAME ON THE JEWS.` · `ASSISI, 1986: SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `NOTHING TRUE IS REJECTED.`

segments.voice: Here is a prayer Jews say every morning and evening, from Deuteronomy, to hear as a guest, not to pray as your own: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Let it sound in you slowly, and think of the people who will say it tonight before they sleep. If you know someone of another faith, think of them too, and of the words they pray, and hold them with respect.
Other religions. How the Catholic Church, since Nostra Aetate in 1965, speaks of other faiths: with respect, rejecting nothing true and holy in them. Today's word.
Your line: nothing true is rejected. Paul started from their altar. That's day three hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Catholic dioceses run interreligious dialogue offices, parishes share service projects and study with neighboring synagogues, mosques and temples, and popes have met leaders of other religions, as at Assisi in 1986.

Review fix: Acts 17:22–23 shows Paul opening from the altar to the unknown god, not with the poets; hook, myth and fork adjusted. That 'in him we live, and move, and are' itself echoes a Greek poet (often credited to Epimenides) is a scholarly view, so the script only credits the poets with 'we are God's offspring' (Aratus), as Acts does.
'One of the shortest documents of the council' and 'many historians count it among the council's most important paragraphs' are softened historical judgments; confirm.
The line 'the Church also keeps proclaiming Christ' reflects Nostra Aetate 2 and is stated as the Church's own position without comparing traditions; Keeper should check tone.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the unsourced 'like most Church documents', 'one of the shortest documents of the council', 'the longest section' and 'many historians count it among the council's most important paragraphs' (claims rule); added the Assisi 1986 gathering to sources. The Shema is quoted in JPS 1917 (not Douay-Rheims) on purpose, because it is presented as the prayer Jews say; Keeper may prefer the Douay-Rheims Deuteronomy 6:4 ('Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord').
